prime.problem: Supervised learning needs the right answer for every example. Once a model has to discover good outputs itself and is only told how good each try was, there is no label to copy, so you need a way to turn a score into a weight update.
prime.fits: Builds on softmax and one gradient step from the z2h cards. This is the RL engine under RLHF (next card) and under GRPO in DeepSeek-R1, whose baseline is the average reward of a group of samples.
expect: REINFORCE: raise log-prob of the sample × its reward
prime.goal: Compute one REINFORCE step on a softmax policy by hand, with and without a baseline, and explain why the baseline keeps the direction but cuts the noise.

attend: Why does plain REINFORCE make a below-average answer more likely when its reward is positive?
What is the vector (one-hot of the sample − probabilities), and why does it point toward the sampled answer?
Why does subtracting a baseline leave the expected step unchanged but shrink the noise of each step?
Why does shifting every reward by +10 wreck learning without a baseline, even though the ranking is the same?
Why does Spinning Up say the policy-gradient "loss" means nothing?

must: No right answer is given → the model samples its own answer → a grader scores it → raise that answer's log-probability in proportion to the score → over many samples, good answers become more likely
Weight = raw reward → every answer with a positive reward is pushed up, including below-average ones → the update is noisy and depends on the reward's arbitrary zero point

Weight = reward − baseline (expected reward) → only better-than-expected answers are pushed up, worse ones down → same expected step ([+0.190, −0.085, −0.105] in the toy) but noise falls from 0.438 to 0.236 → faster, steadier learning

Rewards +10 with no baseline → huge same-sign weights → each run locks onto its early draws (22% of 2,000 toy runs ended over 90% sure of the wrong answer) → with a baseline the +10 cancels and learning is unchanged
elevated: Samples must come from the current policy → after one big step the old samples no longer describe the new policy → that's why PPO limits how far each update moves
With reward 1 on the right answer, always sampled, the REINFORCE gradient equals the cross-entropy gradient → supervised learning is the special case where you're handed the answer
reference: gradient of log softmax wrt the logits = one-hot(sampled) − probabilities
Spinning Up loss in code: -(logp * weights).mean()
Reward-to-go: only rewards after an action should weight it (multi-step episodes)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences how a model can learn from a score instead of a label, and why you subtract a baseline. Or redraw the sketch: three bars, one sample, and the two updates.
checklist: the policy is the model's probabilities; it samples an answer
the update raises the sampled answer's log-probability, scaled by a weight
without a baseline the weight is the raw reward, so any positive reward pushes up
with a baseline the weight is reward minus expected reward, so below-average samples are pushed down
the expected step is the same; only the noise drops

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between what a supervised label tells the model and what a reward tells it.
answer: a label names the right answer, whatever the model did
a reward only scores the answer the model actually produced
so RL must sample, score and reweight instead of copying

retrieve.q: Walk through one REINFORCE step with a baseline for the toy when the model samples “56” (reward 1.0).
answer: logits move by 0.451 × that vector (step size 1)

retrieve.q: You can use the batch's average reward or a learned value model as a baseline. What does each cost, and when would you pick each?
answer: batch or group average: free, no extra model, but needs several samples per prompt (GRPO's choice)
value model: works with one sample per prompt, but is another network to train and can be wrong
either keeps the update unbiased as long as it doesn't depend on the sampled answer

compare.q: Cross-entropy and REINFORCE both change the logits by a multiple of (one-hot − probabilities). What decides which one-hot is used and how big the multiple is in each, and when does each fail?
answer: cross-entropy: the one-hot is the true label, multiple always 1
REINFORCE: the one-hot is the model's own sample, multiple is the reward (minus baseline)
cross-entropy fails without labels; REINFORCE fails when good answers are rarely sampled or the reward is noisy or gameable

compare.q: GRPO samples a group of answers per prompt and subtracts the group's average reward. How is that the same idea as this card's baseline, and what does it save?
answer: it's a baseline: the expected reward estimated from the group
only better-than-group answers are pushed up
it saves training a separate value model

predict.q: Suppose every reward in the toy were negative: right −1, wrong −2, dodge −1.7. With no baseline, what happens to whichever answer is sampled, and does the expected step change?
predict.answer: Whatever is sampled gets pushed down, even the right answer, so single steps are noisy in the other direction. The expected step is the same as before, because shifting all rewards by a constant doesn't change it; a baseline would remove the shift entirely.

apply.task: Using the toy (logits [1.0, 0.0, 1.0], rewards [1.0, 0.0, 0.3]), compute one REINFORCE step with step size 1 when the model samples “56”, once without and once with the baseline of 0.549. Check your softmax with a few lines of numpy.
apply.done: Without a baseline you get probabilities about [0.647, 0.114, 0.238]; with it, about [0.526, 0.139, 0.335].

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: should the dodge with reward 0.3 have gone up or down?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the baseline doesn't bias the step, or why it cuts the noise?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: reward → weight, or weight → change in probabilities?
Where else have you seen a raw score reward something just because it happened?
What would break if the right answer started with probability 0.001?
